text: Chun-Chuan Lin
Designed a trust layer for how Rightmove matches agents with consumers
A self-directed concept. It replaces a checklist of paid agents with a ranking sellers can understand, and keeps paid placement in the business model.
Nov 2026 | Self-directed concept · Flow audit, product strategy, coded prototype
Summary

Rightmove's valuation flow says you'll get a visit from local agents you choose. In practice, you get a list where every agent is already ticked and every one has paid to be there. I used that gap to work through what a Lead Product Designer on Rightmove's Partners team would need to solve.

item: 🔗 Looked at both sides
Sellers have nothing to compare agents on. Agents can only stand out by paying more.
⚖️ Three directions compared
I explored three different approaches and picked one, with reasons.
🧩 A full flow
Five seller screens and three agent screens, built as a clickable prototype.
💷 Revenue kept
Agents can still pay for placement. It's just labelled clearly and kept separate from the ranking.

text: Role: self-directed, solo. Based only on Rightmove's public pages. I had no internal data, and this isn't something Rightmove is building.
The Problem
Before designing anything, I went through the live flow on my phone, choosing the in-home valuation option.

cap: rightmove.co.uk/agent-valuation, captured Nov 2026. Steps 3 to 5 are on one page. When you scroll down to the agents, they're already ticked.

item: 🔗 For sellers: no real choice
All six agents are ticked and labelled Sponsored. There's nothing to tell them apart.
💷 For agents: pay or go unseen
Paying is the only way to appear. There's no free way in.

cap: The last step of the live flow. Six agents, all Sponsored, all ticked before you read their names.

text: So neither side has a way to build trust. This is the same problem the job description describes: “helping consumers feel more confident when choosing an estate agent, while helping agents demonstrate the value they offer.”
Alternatives Considered
I wanted three directions that were actually different, so the choice between them would mean something.

cap: Three concepts, compared on the same four questions.

dd: I chose the hybrid ranking. It didn't win on every measure, but it was the only one that could ship in stages and be tested with little risk. I also kept the best idea from the transparency-first option: agents can see exactly how their score is calculated.

text: The Approach
Paying should decide where an agent appears, not whether a seller trusts them. I'd release this in three phases.

item: 🚦 Phase 1: Stop the list being 100% paid
Rightmove already labels these agents Sponsored. What's missing is a list of agents who didn't pay, and boxes that start unticked.
📈 Phase 2: Add a ranking based on performance
Time to sell, price achieved and reply time. Agents without an ad budget get a way to compete.
🎯 Phase 3: Link the two
Agents with a high score pay less per lead, so both sides benefit from good service.

text: The Prototype
I built the whole seller journey in code, so it can be clicked through, not just looked at.
Each screen answers one question. Who should I pick? Why them? Who else is there? Who gets my phone number?

cap: The seller's journey, recorded from the prototype.
Five screens replace the pre-ticked page. The postcode and valuation-type steps stay as they are.

text: 1 · One recommendation instead of a checklist

item: 🎯 One agent, one button
Most sellers can stop here. Choosing takes one tap.
🧭 Reasons in plain words
How many similar flats they sold nearby, the price they got, and how fast. No star ratings.
🚦 Nothing ticked in advance
No agent gets the request until the seller picks one.

text: 2 · A score you can check

item: 📊 Three measures
Price, speed and reply time. Agents see the same three numbers about themselves.
⚖️ Paid is labelled
If a sponsored agent is opened, the sheet shows where it ranks on performance alone.

text: 3 · Comparing is optional

item: 💷 Sponsored still comes first
It's labelled, scored like everyone else, and shows its real rank.
🎚️ Sort, then pick up to three
Fewer requests, so each one is worth more to the agent who gets it.

text: 4 · Contact details come last

item: 🔗 Choose first, then share
In the current flow you type your phone number before you see the agents.
🧑‍⚖️ Clear about who gets them
The screen and the button both name the agents who will receive the request.

text: The agent side
Agents see the same score from their side, so the design works for both groups, not just sellers.

cap: Value Profile: the agent's score, the one thing to improve, and how much that would move their rank.
Leads: how each seller found the agent, and that the request went to 2 agents, not 6.
Placement: agents can still pay for the top spot, and a higher score makes it cheaper. Prices are illustrative.

text: Leading This
Before anyone built this, I'd raise these points with the team:

item: 🧭 With Research & Data
Rewarding accurate valuations could push agents to quote low on purpose. A score based on past sales also makes it harder for new, small agents, who are the ones this is meant to help.
⚖️ With Commercial & Legal

If sellers contact 2 agents instead of 6, each paying agent gets fewer leads. Whether a chosen lead is worth more needs testing with Revenue. Ranking agents also means Rightmove is recommending them, which has legal implications.
🎯 A decision I'd defend
I didn't design a Yelp-style comparison page. This flow exists to generate leads, so it shows one recommendation first and keeps comparison optional.

text: Reflection
This is a concept and hasn't been tested. The problem is real, but no seller or agent has used the solution yet.

bullets: Test the prototype with sellers against the current flow, and measure how many finish
Check the score against real agent results before using it to rank anyone
Review the pricing model with the team responsible for Premium Listings
See whether agents start gaming the score once it affects their ranking

text: Why it's in my portfolio

My other case studies show work I shipped with real teams. This one shows how I approach a problem from the outside: understand it properly, explore real options, choose one, and be honest about the risks.
